article: Identifying River Rocks by Color, Pattern, and Density
status: All four mandatory materials have identified real photographs and individually verified CC0 permission.
notes: These are separate reference specimens and one limestone locality close-up. They do not show the same stone before/after river wear or wetting.
No reliable commercially reusable photograph documented as a river-worn example was selected for these four materials. No specimen was relabeled as a river find.

The first limestone image comes from a Smithsonian record with four media assets; its exact first asset identifier is retained. General Smithsonian metadata CC0 is not substituted for the selected image usage license.
GeoDIL is a geological teaching image library established with material shared at the University of North Dakota and elsewhere; each selected record separately links CC0.

photos.context: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History reference specimen, Inyo County, California. Not documented as a river find.

photos.caption: Limestone reference specimen, Smithsonian NMNH 91536, from Inyo County, California. Notice the pale, fine-grained surface and narrow intersecting grooves; this is a collection specimen, not a river find.
photos.alt: Pale fine-grained limestone specimen with narrow intersecting grooves and a darker side, on a dark background.
photos.visibleFeature: Pale, mostly uniform fine-grained surface; narrow intersecting grooves; darker exposed side.
photos.visualInspection: Downloaded JPEG visually inspected with view_image. Whole slab visible with black margins and brown display background. No coral fossils or individual calcite crystals claimed. Unusual groove pattern described only as visible grooves; no unverified cause or mineral assignment.
photos.processing: Full frame retained; EXIF rotation applied if present; resized inside a 1400-pixel or 560-pixel square without enlargement; encoded WebP, quality 91 / 88. No crop, generative edit, recoloring, or sharpening.

photos.specimenIdentity: Mississippian-age corals from the lower St. Louis Limestone, near Blue Spring, Trigg County, Kentucky; Joseph Hartman C8769; GeoDIL 2161.
photos.context: Close-up of coral-bearing limestone at the documented Kentucky locality, view parallel to corallites. No river transport asserted.

license.evidence: The individual record contains a copyright table row linking to https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/ with the zero.svg license icon. This was checked in the actual downloaded HTML; GeoDIL copyright policy explicitly says some images are not freely licensed, so the per-image icon, not the site alone, is the approval evidence.

photos.caption: A different limestone example: coral fossils in the St. Louis Limestone near Blue Spring, Kentucky. The closely packed fossil outlines interrupt the fine-grained rock; many limestones do not show fossils this clearly.
photos.alt: Close view of pale limestone containing many closely packed rounded fossil coral outlines.
photos.visibleFeature: Closely packed pale circular to irregular coral outlines within gray-white fine-grained limestone.
photos.visualInspection: Downloaded JPEG visually inspected with view_image. Close-up light gray-white rock shows numerous repeated coral outlines and cracks across its upper edge. Context described as documented limestone locality, not rounded river cobble or same specimen as Smithsonian image.
photos.processing: Full frame retained; EXIF rotation applied if present; resized inside a 1400-pixel or 560-pixel square without enlargement; encoded WebP, quality 91 / 88. No crop, generative edit, recoloring, or sharpening.

photos.caption: Quartz mineral reference specimen from near Cripple Creek, Colorado, about 5 cm long. The crystal has a point at each end and visible faces; it is not a photographed river pebble.

photos.caption: Pale chert from near Joplin, Missouri, about 9 cm across. The curved broken surfaces and very fine texture are useful clues; other cherts can be red, brown, gray, or nearly black.
photos.alt: Pale cream and gray chert hand specimen with curved shell-like broken surfaces and two collection labels.
photos.visibleFeature: Very fine uniform texture with curved shell-like fractured faces; pale cream-gray variation within one specimen.
photos.visualInspection: Downloaded JPEG visually inspected with view_image. Complete irregular pale hand specimen visible on black with collection labels 56. Curved fractures clearly readable. No sand-sized visible grains claimed; label retained and no river-worn classification asserted.

photos.caption: Greenstone reference specimen from near Ely, Minnesota, 8 cm across. Notice the greenish-gray, fine-grained rock; individual minerals cannot be identified by eye in this example. This is a different locality from Shenandoah.
photos.alt: Greenish-gray fine-grained greenstone hand specimen with pale narrow streaks and a blue collection label marked 198.
photos.visibleFeature: Greenish-gray fine-grained surface, narrow pale streaks, and blue and white collection labels.
photos.visualInspection: Downloaded JPEG visually inspected with view_image. Entire angular greenish-gray hand specimen visible with labels 198, pale streaks, rough broken margins. The source expressly says minerals are too fine to identify in hand sample or thin section; no specific visible chlorite or epidote crystals claimed.
